physical.title: Neckpiece with panel (umphapheni)
physical.medium_raw: Glass beads, plant fiber, copper alloy, and iron
physical.summary: Consisting of a tasseled length attached to a rectangular panel joined by metal buttons, this neckpiece (umphapheni) was likely worn along with waistbands and headpieces with the same color scheme and patterns. Joined together using stitches and zig-zag patterns popular around the turn of the 20th century, glass beadwork was heavy to wear. The fringe—typical of Zulu-style Northern Nguni beadwork—added additional weight. The imported glass beads testify to centuries of trade connections between southern Africa and Europe, while the brass buttons—probably drawn from a British soldier’s uniform—allude to the Anglo-Zulu conflicts of the 1800s.

physical.title: Necklace (amazipho)
physical.summary: When wild game was still plentiful in the region, real animal claws would have been used to punctuate beaded prestige necklaces. Lion-claw necklaces were the exclusive property of royalty while the bone imitations were owned and worn by high-ranking individuals of lesser status. Large red glass beads were also reserved for the Nguni elite in the period before the destruction of the Zulu kingdom in 1879.

cultural.vision_reason: The image shows a carved bone snuff spoon/hairpin with incised geometric decoration, a well-documented Zulu personal ornament worn in the hair, consistent with both the claimed ethnicity and category.

physical.title: Snuff Spoon (intshengula or izintshengula)
physical.summary: Often, snuff spoons made from the rib of an ox or cow were subtly carved to suggest a female body. Decorated with incised designs blackened with cattle fat and ash, many are true hybrid objects, combining a spoon with a long-tined comb or hairpin. Such spoons were typically worn as ornaments in the hair or even the beard, thus signaling the social standing of their wearer.

physical.title: Beaded necklace for Zulu girls, 'Love Letter

location.current_museum: National Museum of World Cultures Foundation

dataProvider: National Museum of World Cultures Foundation
dcDescription: The necklace consists of a cord set with white and pink glass beads from which five almost square bead works hang. The five bead works were made according to the so-called 'Baustein-technik' (Lemaire, 1960: 216 and Chater, 1931: 60). These bead works have a similar pattern of white, black and green beads and are finished underneath with red beads. At the clasp, there are two short openwork beaded works on either side in the same colour scheme. These two side parts are made via the 'open net connection' (Lemaire, 1960: 217, fig. 16, p. 230). The clasp itself is formed by two strings of beads, ending in a loop which probably had to be passed over a button (missing) on the other side. \The necklace was worn by Zulu girls who could convey certain messages to their beloved through the different colors. Caution is advised in 'translating' these messages, as there is no single meaning for the colors. There are cultural and regional variations, and the meaning can also vary per family. \However, the coloring of this piece of jewelry could mean the following: \（"I love you" (white), ‖ but there are difficulties‖. (black) ‖ because you don't have cattle for the bride price‖ (pink) and ‖ because you don't have cattle for the bride price‖ (pink). (pink) and \"that's why I feel weak and sick" (green). \Æ "I have red eyes from peering but you won't come" (red) and "I wish I were a pigeon, then I'd come and pick crumbs at your door" (blue).

Het halssieraad bestaat uit een met witte en roze glaskralen bezet koord waaraan vijf bijna vierkante kralenwerken hangen. De vijf kralenwerken zijn gemaakt volgens de zgn. 'Baustein-technik' (Lemaire, 1960: 216 en Chater, 1931: 60) Deze kralenwerken hebben eenzelfde patroon van witte, zwarte en groene kralen en zijn aan de onderzijde afgewerkt met rode kralen. Bij de sluiting zijn aan weerszijden twee korte opengewerkte kralenwerken aangebracht in dezelfde kleurstelling. Deze twee zijgedeelten zijn vervaardigd via de 'open netverbinding' (Lemaire, 1960: 217, fig. 16, p. 230). De sluiting zelf wordt gevormd door twee kralensnoeren, eindigend in een lus die waarschijnlijk over een knoopje (ontbreekt) aan de andere zijde geslagen diende te worden. 

Het halssieraad werd gedragen door Zulu-meisjes die door middel van de verschillende kleuren hun geliefde bepaalde boodschappen konden overbrengen. Voorzichtigheid is geboden bij het 'vertalen' van de boodschappen omdat er geen eenduidige betekenis van de kleuren bestaat, zo zijn er naast culturele ook regionale variaties en kan de betekenis ook per familie varieëren. 
De kleurstelling van dit sieraad zou echter het volgende kunnen betekenen: "Ik heb je lief" (wit), "maar er zijn moeilijkheden" (zwart) "omdat je geen vee hebt voor de bruidsprijs" (roze) en "daarom voel ik me slap en ziek" (groen). "Ik heb rode ogen van het turen maar je komt niet" (rood) en "ik wou dat ik een duif was, dan kwam ik kruimels pikken bij je deur" (blauw).

cultural.vision_reason: A rectangular beaded band ornament with zigzag pattern and shell/pearl button trim, plausibly a Zulu beadwork ornament (belt or necklace piece) as the museum notes; beadwork of this style is consistent with Southern African traditions.

location.current_museum: National Museum of World Cultures Foundation

dataProvider: National Museum of World Cultures Foundation
dcDescription: The ornament in the form of an oblong and rectangular band is made of white beads with one black and two red zigzag lines. On three sides the band is trimmed with pearl or porcelain buttons. Perhaps originating from the Zulu.ManufactureThe rectangular beaded band is strung according to the so-called building stone connection in a zigzag pattern. Three sides are completely trimmed with mother of pearl or porcelain buttons. The fourth side is decorated with blue beads and only in the middle there are two mother-of-pearl buttons sewn on which hang two small beads. On one side there is a string of beads attached to hang the jewellery.

Het sieraad in de vorm van een langwerpige en rechthoekige band is opgebouwd uit witte kralen met  één zwarte en twee rode zigzag-lijnen. Aan drie zijden is de band afgezet met parelmoeren of porseleinen knoopjes. Misschien afkomstig van de Zulu.

Vervaardiging
De rechthoekige kralenband is geregen volgens de zgn. bouwsteen verbinding in een zigzag patroon. Drie zijden zijn geheel afgezet met parelmoeren of porseleinen knoopjes. De vierde zijde is afgezet met blauwe kraaltjes en alleen in het midden hiervan zijn twee parelmoeren knoopjes aangenaaid waaraan twee kleine kralensnoertjes hangen. Aan één zijde is een kralensnoer bevestigd waarmee het sieraad omgehangen zou kunnen worden.
